title: What is the topic proliferation problem in Kafka — as routing needs grow (by type × country × city), the number of flat topics grows very fast, each needing creation, partition sizing, and management — and how does Solace avoid this (one hierarchical topic space, consumers just change their subscription pattern)?
shortTitle: What is the topic proliferation problem in Kafka, and how does Solace avoid it?

s1_definition.profdef: Topic proliferation is the operational problem in Kafka where, because the broker can only route at the granularity of a whole flat topic, the number of topics you must create grows multiplicatively with the number of routing dimensions. If you want to route by three dimensions such as type, country, and city, you end up needing roughly type times country times city topics, each of which must be explicitly created, sized for partitions and replication, monitored, retained, and governed. Solace avoids this because its topic space is a single hierarchical namespace and routing is a subscription-time concern, so adding a new routing need is just a new subscription pattern, not a new broker object.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India wants a separate physical mailbox for every combination of transaction type, branch city, and amount band. With three types, fifty branches, and four amount bands you suddenly need six hundred mailboxes, each installed, labelled, locked, and inspected by the facilities team. That is Kafka topic proliferation. Solace instead has one smart sorting room: every letter is addressed hierarchically, and a desk that wants a new slice just tells the sorting clerk a new address pattern. No new mailbox is ever built; the clerk simply matches addresses on the fly.
s1_definition.oneliner: In Kafka routing lives in the number of topics, so routing dimensions multiply topics; in Solace routing lives in the subscription pattern, so dimensions cost nothing structurally.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Topic proliferation is the operational problem in Kafka where, because the broker can only route at the granularity of a whole flat topic, the number of topics you must create grows multiplicatively with the number of routing dimensions. If you want to route by three dimensions such as type, country, and city, you end up needing roughly type times country times city topics, each of which must be explicitly created, sized for partitions and replication, monitored, retained, and governed. Solace avoids this because its topic space is a single hierarchical namespace and routing is a subscription-time concern, so adding a new routing need is just a new subscription pattern, not a new broker object.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India wants a separate physical mailbox for every combination of transaction type, branch city, and amount band. With three types, fifty branches, and four amount bands you suddenly need six hundred mailboxes, each installed, labelled, locked, and inspected by the facilities team. That is Kafka topic proliferation. Solace instead has one smart sorting room: every letter is addressed hierarchically, and a desk that wants a new slice just tells the sorting clerk a new address pattern. No new mailbox is ever built; the clerk simply matches addresses on the fly.

**One line to remember:** In Kafka routing lives in the number of topics, so routing dimensions multiply topics; in Solace routing lives in the subscription pattern, so dimensions cost nothing structurally.

sections.s2_technical:
Kafka routes at topic granularity. The broker does not look inside a record, so the only way for a consumer to receive just a subset of data without downloading everything is for that subset to already be its own topic. This forces the routing decision to publish time: the publisher must decide which fine-grained topic a record belongs to and write it there.

The moment you have more than one routing dimension, the topic count becomes a product. Suppose you route transactions by type (credit, debit, transfer), by country (IN, BR, US, UK), and by amount band (small, medium, large). That is three times four times three, which is thirty-six topics, and it was only three small dimensions. Real systems have dozens of branches and many categories, so the count reaches hundreds or thousands quickly. Each topic is not free: it needs a creation step (often gated by a platform team), a partition count chosen for its expected throughput, a replication factor, retention settings, ACLs, and monitoring for under-replicated partitions and consumer lag. A cluster has a practical ceiling on total partitions because each partition consumes broker memory, file handles, and controller metadata, so uncontrolled topic growth can destabilise the cluster.

There is a second pain: change. If the business adds a fourth amount band or a new country, you must create a new set of topics, update producer routing logic, update ACLs, and tell consumers to subscribe to the new topics. Routing logic is now baked into topic structure, which is the hardest thing to change in a running Kafka estate.

Teams mitigate this in several ways, none free. One mitigation is to keep topics coarse, such as one `transactions` topic, and filter in consumers; this trades topic sprawl for consumer CPU and network waste, since every consumer reads everything. Another is to add a stream-processing layer with Kafka Streams or ksqlDB that reads a coarse topic and dynamically branches into narrower topics, which centralises the routing but adds a stateful service you must operate and scale. A third is a hybrid where a few high-value slices get their own topics and the long tail is filtered client-side.

Solace avoids the problem by making the topic a publish-time string in a single hierarchical namespace rather than a pre-created broker object. There is no `createTopic` step for each combination; the publisher just writes a richly structured topic string like transaction, then country, then type, then band. Routing is entirely a subscriber concern expressed with wildcards. A desk that wants Brazil large transactions subscribes with a pattern pinning the country and band levels; a desk that wants everything from Mumbai subscribes with a multi-level wildcard under Mumbai. Adding a new routing need is a new subscription pattern registered by the consumer, and adding a new dimension value such as a new country requires no broker change at all because any topic string is instantly routable. The broker's trie-based matcher handles arbitrary combinations without any pre-provisioning.

The senior nuance is that this is a genuine trade-off, not a free win. Solace pays with broker-side matching CPU and with the fact that its hierarchical persistence and replay story is different from Kafka's partitioned log. Kafka's flat log gives it unmatched sequential throughput, ordered partitions, long retention, and replay, which are exactly why banks keep Kafka as the durable backbone even when Solace handles the live fan-out. So the practical answer to proliferation is often not to force Kafka to route finely, but to let Solace route and let Kafka store.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India wants to distribute its live transaction feed to many desks, each wanting a different slice defined by transaction type, country, and amount band.

Problem 1 — The platform team notices that giving every desk its own Kafka topic means creating type times country times band topics. When the business opened operations in two new countries, the number of topics jumped again, and each new topic needed partitions, replication, ACLs, and a dashboard. This is exactly the topic proliferation problem: routing dimensions multiply topic count, and every topic is an operational object.

Problem 2 — A new compliance rule arrives mid-quarter: a "very large" amount band must be tracked separately. In the Kafka-per-combination design this means creating a whole new row of topics across every type and country and rewiring producers. This is exactly why routing baked into topic structure is painful to change.

Problem 3 — The architecture team asks: what if routing were a subscription pattern instead of a topic? Then a new band is just a new subscription string, no broker objects created. This is exactly how Solace's single hierarchical namespace avoids proliferation.

The demo models both worlds. A `KafkaTopicPlanner` computes and "creates" the cartesian set of topics for given dimensions and reports the count and the operational cost. A `SolaceNamespace` publishes into one hierarchical space and lets desks register patterns, showing that adding a dimension value or a new desk costs zero new topics. The `main` method first sizes the Kafka topic explosion for three dimensions, then adds a fourth band and shows the explosion grow, then shows Solace absorbing the same requirements with only new subscription strings.

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  application:
    name: topic-strategy-service
kafka:
  default-partitions: 6        # each created topic needs partition sizing
  replication-factor: 3        # each created topic needs replicas
  max-cluster-partitions: 200000  # practical ceiling to respect
solace:
  msgVpn: txn-vpn
  # no per-combination topic creation needed
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/topic-strategy-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.routing.TopicStrategyDemo

# In real Kafka each planned topic would be created with:
# kafka-topics.sh --create --topic txn.credit.BR.large --partitions 6 --replication-factor 3 \
#   --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092
```

##### 4f. Logging notes

Topic creation is logged at `fine` so the sheer number is visible without flooding `info`; the warning level is used when adding one dimension value causes the topic count to jump, which is the moment proliferation bites.
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three transaction types, four countries, three amount bands, plus a later fourth band for compliance.

Step 1: The Kafka planner walks the cartesian product of three types, four countries, and three bands. It "creates" three times four times three, which is thirty-six topics. Each topic is logged with its partition and replication settings.

Step 2: The planner reports that thirty-six topics need thirty-six times six, which is two hundred and sixteen partitions provisioned, each consuming broker metadata and file handles.

Step 3: Compliance adds a fourth band. The planner reruns with four bands and now produces three times four times four, which is forty-eight topics, a jump of twelve new topics. The demo logs a warning because this also means rewiring producers, adding ACLs, and creating dashboards for the new topics.

Step 4: The Solace path starts. Three desks register subscription patterns: Brazil large, everything India, and a new very-large monitor. The namespace reports zero topics created and three subscriptions registered.

Step 5: A message with topic `txn/BR/transfer/large` is published. The namespace tests each pattern: the Brazil-large desk matches on country BR and band large, so it is delivered; the India desk fails on country; the very-large monitor fails on band. One matching desk receives it, and no topic had to exist beforehand.

Step 6: A message with topic `txn/IN/credit/veryLarge` is published. The India desk matches via its multi-level wildcard; the very-large monitor matches via its band pin. Two desks receive it. The brand-new band value `veryLarge` worked instantly with zero broker changes, which is the whole point.

```
23:14:51 INFO    === KAFKA per-combination topics ===

23:14:51 WARNING After adding one band: topics jump from 36 to 48 (rewire producers + ACLs + dashboards)
23:14:51 INFO    === SOLACE single hierarchical namespace ===
23:14:51 INFO    subscribe brazil-large-desk -> txn/BR/*/large (no topic created)
23:14:51 INFO    subscribe mumbai-ops-desk -> txn/IN/> (no topic created)
23:14:51 INFO    subscribe verylarge-monitor -> txn/*/*/veryLarge (no topic created)

```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Routing dimensions: types(3) × countries(4) × bands(3)
    │
    ├──────────── KAFKA PATH (topics multiply) ───────────────┐

  KafkaTopicPlanner.planTopics(...)
    │ nested loop over every combination
    │ CREATE txn.credit.IN.small ... txn.transfer.UK.large
    ▼
  36 topics × 6 partitions = 216 partitions provisioned
    │ add 1 band (compliance) ───→ 48 topics  (+12, rewire everything)
    │
    └──────────── SOLACE PATH (patterns only) ────────────────┐
                                                               ▼
  SolaceNamespace (ONE hierarchical space, 0 topics created)
    │ subscribe brazil-large-desk  -> txn/BR/*/large
    │ subscribe mumbai-ops-desk    -> txn/IN/>
    │ subscribe verylarge-monitor  -> txn/*/*/veryLarge   (new rule = 1 sub)
    ▼
  publish txn/IN/credit/veryLarge → matched by trie → delivered
  (new band value worked with ZERO broker objects created)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Topic proliferation is the operational problem in Kafka where the number of topics you must create grows multiplicatively with your routing dimensions. Because the Kafka broker only routes at the granularity of a whole flat topic and never looks inside a record, the only way a consumer can receive just a slice without downloading everything is for that slice to already be its own topic. So if you want to route by type, country, and amount band, you end up needing roughly type times country times band topics, which for even small dimensions becomes dozens, and for real systems becomes hundreds or thousands.

The cost is not just the count. Every Kafka topic needs an explicit creation step that is usually gated by a platform team, a partition count chosen for its throughput, a replication factor, retention settings, access-control lists, and monitoring for under-replicated partitions and consumer lag. Partitions consume broker memory, file handles, and controller metadata, so a cluster has a practical ceiling and uncontrolled topic growth can destabilise it. Worse, routing is now baked into topic structure, so when the business adds one new amount band or one new country you must create a whole new set of topics, rewire producer routing, update ACLs, and tell every consumer about the new topics. Routing structure is the hardest thing to change in a running Kafka estate.

Solace avoids this because its topic is a publish-time string in a single hierarchical namespace rather than a pre-created broker object. There is no per-combination creation step; the publisher simply writes a structured topic such as transaction, then country, then type, then band, and routing is entirely a subscriber concern expressed with level-aware wildcards. A desk that wants Brazil large transactions registers one subscription pattern, and a brand-new amount band required by compliance is just one more subscription string, with zero new topics created and no producer rewiring, because any topic string is instantly routable by the broker's matcher.

At National Bank of India I used this distinction directly. When desks wanted finely sliced live feeds across many combinations of type, country, and band, forcing Kafka to route them would have meant creating and governing hundreds of topics and rebuilding them every time the business added a dimension value, so we let Solace route those live slices through one hierarchical namespace where new needs are just new subscriptions. The senior point I always add is that this is a trade-off rather than a free win: Solace pays with broker-side matching CPU, while Kafka's flat log is exactly what gives it unmatched throughput, ordered partitions, long retention, and replay. So in practice the cleanest answer to proliferation is not to make Kafka route finely but to let Solace route the live fan-out and keep Kafka as the durable, replayable backbone.
